strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: characterizing degrees of human involvement in AI-assisted writing. It explicitly focuses on informational contribution and acknowledges limitations concerning creative effort and copyright.

The known-input score is simple and implementable using conditional and unconditional token likelihoods. Model checkpoints, generation settings, hardware details, dataset links, and a public code link support reproducibility.

The experiments cover four domains, multiple generation and surrogate models, repeated generations, and 2,500 WildChat examples. Consistent trends across these settings provide useful evidence that the score distinguishes broad generation regimes. The human comparison study supplies additional, albeit restricted, validation.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a percentage of human-contributed information is insufficiently established. Equations 1–5 compute a normalized pointwise likelihood gain, which can be negative; negative scores also appear in Figure 7. Moreover, the unprompted model distribution is not shown to be the output marginal of a joint prompt–output distribution. These issues weaken the shared-information interpretation in Figure 1. The evidence supports a prompt-dependence proxy more clearly than calibrated fractional attribution.

The text-only extension has a substantial justification gap. Equation 9 establishes a lower bound conditional on the chosen plausibility threshold; it does not establish that this bound is attainable or accurately estimates the minimum over prompts. Equation 10 simplifies to 1 + log(tau)/(I(y)/N), a monotonic transformation of average unconditional surprisal. The thresholds 0.65 and 0.7 lack a documented calibration procedure, sensitivity analysis, or validation of bound tightness. Consequently, the claim to estimate necessarily human-provided information remains unsupported.

Most experiments validate an assumed ordering of polishing, summary-based generation, title-based generation, and subject-based generation. These conditions also differ greatly in input length and textual overlap. Without length-ratio, overlap, and likelihood baselines or comparisons that control these factors, the experiments do not establish what the proposed measure captures beyond straightforward correlates of the generation regime. WildChat category comparisons retain this limitation.

The reported 97.4% human agreement is conditional on selecting 1,000 pairs whose proposed scores already differ by more than 0.1. This selection excludes close cases and cannot establish agreement on the general population. An independently sampled evaluation, including within-regime comparisons and results stratified by score gap, is needed.

Robustness claims exceed the attack evaluation. Appending two fixed instructions about unusual vocabulary and human-like writing tests limited perturbations, without demonstrating resistance to an adversary optimizing the proposed score. Likewise, preserving aggregate category order under surrogate models does not establish accurate attribution for individual examples.

Reproducibility cannot be fully assessed from the supplied manuscript: sampling procedures, exact prompts, and annotation instructions are deferred to supplementary material that is not included. Annotator agreement and scoring conventions, including chat formatting and treatment of decoding temperature, also need clearer documentation. Together with the central validation gaps, these issues warrant important revisions before a Findings recommendation.
